8. Right to legal aid (Section 27): Right to free legal aid under the Legal Services Authorities Act.
9. Right to complain (Section 28): Right to complain about deficiencies in care.
10. Right to make an Advance Directive (Section 5): A person can specify in advance how they wish to be treated if they lose mental capacity.

**Decriminalisation of suicide attempt:** Section 115 of the Act decriminalises attempt to suicide — it presumes that a person who attempts suicide is under severe stress and must be presumed to be suffering from mental illness. Such a person cannot be punished under Section 226 of the BNS (attempt to suicide). The Government must provide care, treatment, and rehabilitation.

**Electro-Convulsive Therapy (ECT):** Banned for minors. For adults, only with anaesthesia and muscle relaxants, and only in exceptional cases.

**Independent review:** Mental Health Review Boards are established at state level to review admissions and treatment, especially involuntary admissions.

**How to enforce?** 1. Approach the State Mental Health Authority. 2. File a complaint with the Mental Health Review Board. 3. Approach the NHRC (14433). 4. Seek legal aid through DLSA helpline 15100. 5. Contact iCall helpline 9152987821 (free counselling by TISS) or Vandrevala Foundation 1860-2662-345.
actualLaw: Mental Healthcare Act, 2017
example: A person with depression is denied health insurance. This violates Section 21(4) of the Mental Healthcare Act, which prohibits discrimination in insurance on the ground of mental illness.
whatToDoIfViolated:
1. File complaint with the Mental Health Review Board.
2. Approach the State Mental Health Authority.
3. File complaint with the Insurance Regulatory Authority (IRDAI) if insurance is denied.
4. Approach the National Human Rights Commission at 14433.
5. Seek help from NGOs like Sangath or iCall helpline 9152987821.
6. Seek free legal aid through NALSA helpline 15100.

title: Right to Maintenance for Senior Citizens
summary: Senior citizens (60+) and parents who are unable to maintain themselves can claim monthly maintenance from their children or heirs under the Maintenance and Welfare of Parents and Senior Citizens Act 2007.
body:
The **Maintenance and Welfare of Parents and Senior Citizens Act, 2007** (amended in 2023) provides a quick and inexpensive mechanism for senior citizens and parents to claim maintenance from their children or heirs. The Act applies to senior citizens (60 years and above) and parents (regardless of age) who are unable to maintain themselves.

**Who is liable to pay maintenance?** Children (son, daughter, grandson, granddaughter) and, in the absence of children, legal heirs of a deceased child who are major and possess the property. They are liable to pay maintenance if the parent/senior citizen is unable to maintain themselves from their own earnings or property.

**How much can be claimed?** The 2023 amendment removed the earlier cap of ₹10,000 per month. The Maintenance Tribunal can now fix any amount based on the needs of the senior citizen and the income of the children/heirs. The maximum limit is left to the Tribunal's discretion.

**How to claim?** File an application before the Maintenance Tribunal (usually the Sub-Divisional Magistrate or SDM office) of the district where the senior citizen or child resides. The Tribunal must take cognisance on the day of application and pass an interim order within 90 days. The final order must be passed within 90 days of the interim order — making this one of the fastest legal remedies.

**What if the children don't pay?** The Tribunal can issue a warrant for recovery of the amount as if it were an arrears of land revenue. The Tribunal can also order imprisonment up to 1 month for non-payment.

**Protection of property (Section 23):** If a senior citizen has transferred their property (by gift or otherwise) to a child or relative on the condition that they will be taken care of, and the child/relative subsequently neglects or fails to provide care, the senior citizen can declare the transfer void. This is a powerful remedy — it reverses the property transfer.

**Other reliefs available:**
1. Section 144 of the BNS, 2023 (formerly Section 125 CrPC) — maintenance for parents.
2. Senior Citizens Helpline 14567.
3. NALSA helpline 15100 for free legal aid.
4. Old Age Pension Scheme — every state has a scheme for monthly pension to BPL seniors.
5. IGNOAPS (Indira Gandhi National Old Age Pension Scheme) — ₹200 per month (₹500 in some states) for BPL persons aged 60+.

If abandoned or neglected: approach the Maintenance Tribunal immediately. The procedure is simple — you can file the application yourself. Free legal aid is available through DLSA.
actualLaw: Maintenance and Welfare of Parents and Senior Citizens Act, 2007 (as amended in 2023); Section 144, Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (formerly Section 125 CrPC)
example: An elderly parent is abandoned by their son. They can file for monthly maintenance before the Maintenance Tribunal (SDM office) under the MWPSC Act, 2007.
whatToDoIfViolated:
1. File an application before the Maintenance Tribunal (SDM office) of your district.
2. Approach Elders Helpline 14567.
3. File under Section 144 BNS, 2023 for parallel maintenance.
4. Contact NALSA helpline 15100 for free legal aid.
5. Apply for Old Age Pension Scheme in your state.
6. If property transferred, file for declaration of transfer as void under Section 23.

title: Right to Protection of Life and Property
summary: Senior citizens have the right to live in their own property and cannot be evicted by children or relatives. Transfer of property for care can be declared void if care is not provided.
body:
Beyond maintenance, the **Maintenance and Welfare of Parents and Senior Citizens Act, 2007** also protects the life, liberty, and property of senior citizens. **Section 23** of the Act is a key provision that allows senior citizens to reverse property transfers made in exchange for care that was not provided.

**What does Section 23 say?** If a senior citizen transfers property (by gift, will, or any other mode) to a child or relative on the condition that the transferee will provide basic needs and physical needs, and the transferee subsequently fails or refuses to provide such care, the senior citizen can declare the transfer void. The property reverts to the senior citizen.

**Procedure:** The senior citizen can file an application before the Maintenance Tribunal (SDM office) seeking declaration that the transfer is void. The Tribunal can cancel the transfer and restore the property to the senior citizen. This remedy is much faster than a regular civil suit.

**What other protections does the Act provide?**
1. Right to retain possession: Children or relatives cannot evict a senior citizen from the property in which they are living, except through due process of law.
2. Protection against physical/mental abuse: If a senior citizen faces abuse, they can seek a Protection Order from the Tribunal. The Tribunal can also issue Welfare Orders.
3. Establishment of senior citizen homes: The Act mandates State Governments to establish and maintain senior citizen homes (old age homes) — at least one in each district, with a minimum capacity of 150 senior citizens.
4. Medical facilities: The Government must ensure specialised medical facilities for senior citizens, including separate queues in hospitals, geriatric care, and home visits for those who cannot travel.
5. Helplines: Each state must establish a senior citizen helpline (14567 is the national helpline).

**Other related protections:**
1. Reverse mortgage: Senior citizens can avail reverse mortgage loans against their property — they receive monthly payments from the bank and continue to live in the property. The Reverse Mortgage Act, 2007 enables this.
2. Maintenance under Section 144 BNS, 2023 (formerly Section 125 CrPC): Parents who cannot maintain themselves can claim maintenance from their adult children.
3. NALSA helpline 15100: Free legal aid for senior citizens.
4. Police protection: Senior citizens can register their details with the local police station for periodic visits and verification of their welfare.

If facing abuse or illegal eviction: 1. Call 14567 (Senior Citizen Helpline). 2. Approach the Maintenance Tribunal (SDM office) under Section 23 to declare transfer void. 3. File an FIR if physical abuse, criminal trespass, or cheating. 4. File a police complaint for harassment. 5. Approach NHRC at 14433 if human rights violation. 6. Approach the High Court under Article 226 if relief denied.
actualLaw: Section 23, Maintenance and Welfare of Parents and Senior Citizens Act, 2007; Reverse Mortgage Act, 2007
example: A senior citizen transfers property to a son on the promise of lifelong care. The son later evicts them. The transfer can be declared void under Section 23 of the MWPSC Act.
whatToDoIfViolated:
1. Call 14567 (Senior Citizen Helpline).
2. Approach the Maintenance Tribunal (SDM office) under Section 23 to declare transfer void.
3. File an FIR if physical abuse, criminal trespass, or cheating.
4. File a police complaint for harassment.
5. Approach NHRC at 14433 if human rights violation.
6. Approach the High Court under Article 226 if relief denied.

title: Right to Education for Students
summary: Children aged 6-14 have a fundamental right to free and compulsory education. No child can be discriminated against on grounds of religion, caste, gender, or disability.
body:
Education is a fundamental right, not a privilege. **Article 21A** of the Constitution makes free and compulsory education for children aged 6 to 14 years a fundamental right. The **Right of Children to Free and Compulsory Education (RTE) Act, 2009** operationalises this right.

**What rights do students have under the RTE Act and the Constitution?**
1. Right to free education: No fees, capitation fees, or any kind of charges for Class 1-8 in neighbourhood schools (Government and Government-aided schools, and 25% seats in private unaided schools for EWS).
2. Right to non-discrimination: A child cannot be discriminated against on grounds of religion, race, caste, sex, residence, or disability. Dalit children, Muslim girls, children with disabilities — all have equal rights.
3. Right against screening tests: No school can subject the child or parent to any screening test or interview for admission.
4. Right against capitation fees: Charging capitation fees is punishable with a fine up to 10 times the fees charged.
5. Right against corporal punishment: Physical punishment, mental harassment, and discriminatory treatment are prohibited. The Act bans hitting, slapping, ear-pulling, and humiliating a child. The Juvenile Justice Act also prohibits corporal punishment in schools.
6. Right to a safe school environment: Schools must ensure safety of children — including infrastructure, drinking water, toilets (separate for girls and boys), boundary walls, playgrounds, and trained teachers.
7. Right against expulsion: A child cannot be expelled from school until Class 8, except in very limited circumstances, and only after evaluation.
8. Right to a qualified teacher: Teachers must meet minimum qualifications laid down by NCTE. Pupil-teacher ratio (30:1 in primary classes) is mandated.
9. Right to mother tongue education: Medium of instruction should be the child's mother tongue as far as practicable.

For students above Class 8, the Right to Education is not a fundamental right, but the State has a duty under Article 45 (now a Directive Principle) to provide early childhood care and education for children below 6 years.

For higher education: The University Grants Commission (UGC) Act, 1956 and the All India Council for Technical Education (AICTE) Act, 1987 regulate universities and technical institutions. The Right to Education Act does not apply to higher education, but students have rights against arbitrary expulsion, capitation fees, and discrimination.

If a child is denied admission, discriminated against, or faces corporal punishment: 1. File a complaint with the District Education Officer. 2. Approach the State Commission for Protection of Child Rights (SCPCR). 3. Call NCPCR at 1800-121-2830. 4. Approach CHILDLINE 1098. 5. File a writ petition in the High Court under Article 226 for violation of fundamental right.
actualLaw: Article 21A, Constitution of India; Right of Children to Free and Compulsory Education Act, 2009
example: A school denies admission to a child from a marginalised community citing caste. This violates the RTE Act, which prohibits discrimination on grounds of religion, race, caste, sex, or residence.
whatToDoIfViolated:
1. File a complaint with the District Education Officer.
2. Approach the State Commission for Protection of Child Rights (SCPCR).
3. Call NCPCR helpline 1800-121-2830.
4. Approach CHILDLINE 1098.
5. File a writ petition in the High Court under Article 226 for violation of fundamental right.
6. Seek free legal aid from DLSA.

title: Right Against Ragging
summary: Ragging in educational institutions is a criminal offence. Students facing ragging can file a complaint anonymously with the Anti-Ragging Helpline 1800-180-5522 or at antiragging.in.
body:
Ragging — the bullying, harassment, and humiliation of new students by seniors — is a criminal offence in India. Following the death of Aman Kachroo in 2009 due to ragging, the UGC notified strict **Anti-Ragging Regulations, 2009**, which apply to all higher educational institutions.

**What is ragging?** Under the UGC Anti-Ragging Regulations, 2009, ragging includes: teasing, manhandling, handling, abusing, threatening, or playing practical jokes on a student; forcing a student to do an act that causes shame, embarrassment, or physical/mental injury; forcing a student to do menial acts such as washing clothes, fetching water, etc.; any act that adversely affects the physique or psyche of a student; and any act of extortion or intimidation.

**Penalties for ragging:**
1. Punishment under law: Up to 2 years imprisonment and a fine of ₹10,000 (Section 4 of the UGC Regulations, 2009). Where the act also amounts to an offence under BNS, the offender is liable under BNS as well.
2. Institutional punishment: Suspension, expulsion, rustication, debarring from exams, withholding of results, withholding of scholarship, or fine of up to ₹25,000.
3. Collective punishment: If an incident of ragging occurs in a hostel, the entire hostel or class can be collectively punished if individuals cannot be identified.

**What must institutions do?**
1. Constitute an Anti-Ragging Committee (ARC) at the institution level, headed by the Head of the Institution, with faculty, students, and external members.
2. Constitute Anti-Ragging Squads at the department/hostel level for surprise inspections.
3. Obtain an anti-ragging undertaking from every student and parent at the time of admission.
4. Submit regular reports to the UGC.
5. Display anti-ragging posters and helpline numbers prominently.

**How to report ragging?**
1. National Anti-Ragging Helpline: 1800-180-5522 (24x7, toll-free). Call to register complaint — the helpline forwards to the institution's ARC and the UGC.
2. Online complaint at antiragging.in — the portal generates an acknowledgment and tracks the complaint.
3. Approach the Anti-Ragging Committee of your institution — every college must have one.
4. File an FIR at the local police station if the ragging amounts to a criminal offence under BNS (e.g., Section 117 BNS for voluntarily causing hurt, Section 318 for extortion, Section 118 for wrongful confinement, Section 75 for sexual harassment).
5. Approach the National Human Rights Commission at 14433 if human rights violation.
6. Approach the State Commission for Protection of Child Rights if the victim is below 18.

**Confidentiality:** The identity of the complainant is kept confidential. The UGC and the institution must take action without revealing the complainant's identity.
actualLaw: UGC Anti-Ragging Regulations, 2009; relevant sections of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (Section 117 for voluntarily causing hurt, Section 118 for wrongful confinement, Section 318 for extortion, Section 75 for sexual harassment)
example: A first-year college student is subjected to physical and mental abuse by seniors in a hostel. They can file a complaint with the Anti-Ragging Committee or call 1800-180-5522.
whatToDoIfViolated:
1. Call National Anti-Ragging Helpline 1800-180-5522 (24x7, toll-free).
2. File an online complaint at antiragging.in.
3. Approach the Anti-Ragging Committee of your institution.
4. File an FIR under BNS if the act amounts to a criminal offence.
5. Approach the NHRC at 14433 if human rights violation.
6. Approach the SCPCR if the victim is below 18.

title: Right to Information (RTI)
summary: Every citizen has the right to obtain information from any public authority. The fee is ₹10 and the authority must respond within 30 days (48 hours for life and liberty).
body:
The **Right to Information Act, 2005 (RTI Act)** is one of the most powerful tools for citizen empowerment in India. It gives every citizen the right to obtain information from any 'public authority' — any body owned, controlled, or substantially financed by the Government, including Government departments, public sector undertakings, universities, and even some private bodies substantially funded by the Government.

**What information can you ask for?** You can ask for copies of files, documents, memos, emails, opinions, advices, press releases, circulars, contracts, samples, or any material in any electronic or physical form held by a public authority. You can also inspect works, documents, and records, and take samples of materials.

**What information is exempt?** Section 8 of the Act lists exemptions — information that would prejudicially affect sovereignty, strategic interests, security, relations with foreign states, Cabinet papers (until decisions are taken), trade secrets, information received in confidence from a foreign government, information that would endanger life, and certain personal information. However, even exempt information must be disclosed if public interest outweighs the harm.

**How to file an RTI application?**
1. Identify the public authority that holds the information.
2. File a written application (or online at rtionline.gov.in for Central Government authorities; many states have their own online portals).
3. Pay the application fee of ₹10 (free for BPL applicants — they must attach BPL certificate).
4. Submit the application to the Public Information Officer (PIO) of the public authority. You do not need to give reasons for seeking information.

**Time limits:**
1. 30 days from receipt of application (48 hours if life or liberty is involved).
2. 35 days if the application is transferred to another public authority.
3. 40 days if the information concerns a third party.

If the PIO does not respond within 30 days, or refuses information wrongly, you can file: 1. First Appeal with the First Appellate Authority (FAA) of the same public authority — within 30 days of the PIO's response or non-response (extendable to 90 days). 2. Second Appeal with the Central Information Commission (cic.gov.in) or State Information Commission within 90 days of the FAA's order.

**Penalties:** The Information Commission can impose a penalty of ₹250 per day on the PIO (up to ₹25,000) for delay without reasonable cause, and recommend disciplinary action.

RTI has exposed scams (2G spectrum, Adarsh, Commonwealth Games), forced disclosure of assets of judges and ministers, and is a powerful tool for accountability.
actualLaw: Right to Information Act, 2005
example: A citizen wants to know the status of their ration card application. They can file an RTI application with the Food Department paying a fee of ₹10, and must get a reply within 30 days.
whatToDoIfViolated:
1. File an RTI application online (rtionline.gov.in) or with the Public Information Officer (PIO).
2. Pay the ₹10 fee (free for BPL applicants — attach BPL certificate).
3. Wait 30 days for response (48 hours for life and liberty).
4. If no response or wrong denial, file First Appeal within 30 days.
5. If unsatisfied, file Second Appeal before the Central/State Information Commission within 90 days.
6. Seek free legal aid from DLSA if required.

title: RTI First and Second Appeal
summary: If a PIO does not respond or denies information wrongly, the applicant can file a First Appeal. If still unsatisfied, a Second Appeal can be filed with the Information Commission.
body:
If a Public Information Officer (PIO) does not respond to your RTI application within the prescribed time, or denies information wrongly, the **Right to Information Act, 2005** provides a two-tier appeal mechanism — the First Appeal and the Second Appeal.

**When to file a First Appeal?**
- The PIO did not respond within 30 days (or 48 hours for life and liberty matters).
- The PIO refused information claiming an exemption that you believe does not apply.
- The PIO gave incomplete, misleading, or false information.
- The PIO charged excessive fees.

**How to file a First Appeal?**
1. Identify the First Appellate Authority (FAA) of the same public authority. Every public authority must designate an FAA — usually a senior officer one level above the PIO.
2. File a written appeal (no fee required) within 30 days of the PIO's response (or non-response). The time limit can be extended to 90 days if sufficient cause is shown.
3. The FAA must dispose of the appeal within 30 days (extendable to 45 days) of receipt, with reasons recorded in writing.

The FAA can order the PIO to provide the information, modify the PIO's decision, or uphold the PIO's decision.

**When to file a Second Appeal?**
- The FAA did not respond within 45 days.
- The FAA upheld the PIO's decision and you believe it is wrong.
- The FAA ordered the PIO to provide information but the PIO has still not complied.

**How to file a Second Appeal?**
1. File a written appeal before the Central Information Commission (CIC) for Central Government authorities, or the State Information Commission for State Government authorities.
2. The Second Appeal must be filed within 90 days of the FAA's decision (extendable if sufficient cause is shown).
3. The Information Commission can summon the PIO, examine records, order disclosure of information, impose penalties on the PIO (₹250 per day up to ₹25,000), and recommend disciplinary action.
4. The Information Commission's decision is binding, but a writ petition can be filed in the High Court under Article 226 if dissatisfied.

**Important tips:**
- Keep copies of every application, response, and appeal.
- Mention the dates of each communication — the Act is strict about timelines.
- You do not need a lawyer for either appeal.
- For online filing, use the CIC portal (cic.gov.in) or your state's Information Commission portal.
- The Second Appeal is free of cost.

RTI is a citizen's most powerful tool against government opacity — use it assertively.
actualLaw: Section 19, Right to Information Act, 2005
example: A PIO denies information about expenditure of public funds citing 'internal matter'. The applicant can file a First Appeal with the First Appellate Authority within 30 days.
whatToDoIfViolated:
1. File First Appeal within 30 days of PIO's response (or non-response) with the First Appellate Authority of the same public authority.
2. Wait 30-45 days for the FAA's decision.
3. If unsatisfied, file Second Appeal before the Central Information Commission (cic.gov.in) or State Information Commission within 90 days.
4. The Information Commission can impose penalties and order disclosure.
5. If still unsatisfied, file a writ petition in the High Court under Article 226.

title: Right to a Safe Workplace
summary: Every worker has the right to a safe and healthy workplace, free from occupational hazards and sexual harassment. Employers must provide protective equipment, training, and a grievance mechanism.
body:
Every worker in India has the right to a workplace that is safe, healthy, and free from harassment. The **Occupational Safety, Health and Working Conditions Code, 2020 (OSH Code)** consolidates earlier labour laws on workplace safety, while the **Sexual Harassment of Women at Workplace (Prevention, Prohibition and Redressal) Act, 2013 (POSH Act)** protects women from sexual harassment at work.

**Duties of the employer under the OSH Code, 2020:**
1. Provide a safe workplace free from risk of injury or illness.
2. Provide **personal protective equipment (PPE)** — helmets, safety shoes, gloves, goggles, harnesses — at no cost to the worker.
3. Conduct regular safety training and display safety signage in the local language.
4. Maintain first-aid facilities, fire-fighting equipment, and emergency exits.
5. Appoint a **Safety Officer** in establishments with 500+ workers (and other high-hazard industries).
6. Report any workplace accident causing death or serious bodily injury to the Inspector-cum-Facilitator and the worker's family.
7. Provide drinking water, washrooms (separate for men and women), canteens (where 250+ workers), and crèches (where 50+ women workers).
8. Limit working hours to 8 per day and 48 per week, with a mandatory weekly off.

**POSH Act protections (2013):**
1. Applies to all workplaces — organised and unorganised, public and private.
2. Mandatory **Internal Complaints Committee (ICC)** for establishments with 10+ employees; **Local Complaints Committee (LCC)** at the district level for smaller workplaces.
3. The ICC must have a woman chairperson, at least half women members, and an external member from an NGO.
4. Complaints can be filed within 3 months of the incident (extendable to 6 months).
5. Conciliation is optional; if it fails, an inquiry is conducted within 90 days.
6. The employer must act on the ICC report within 60 days.
7. Identity of the complainant and witnesses is confidential.
8. False or malicious complaints are punishable, but a wrong complaint made in good faith is not punished.

**Hazardous industries (mines, factories, construction):** The OSH Code and the Building and Other Construction Workers (Regulation of Employment and Conditions of Service) Act, 1996 impose additional duties — fall protection, scaffolding, electrical safety, hazardous chemical handling, and reporting of accidents.

If injured at work: the employee is entitled to compensation under the **Employees' Compensation Act, 1923** — calculated as a percentage of wages based on the extent of disability and age. ESIC-covered workers claim through ESIC.
actualLaw: Occupational Safety, Health and Working Conditions Code, 2020; Sexual Harassment of Women at Workplace (Prevention, Prohibition and Redressal) Act, 2013; Employees' Compensation Act, 1923
example: A factory worker is not given safety gloves and suffers a hand injury. The employer is liable to pay compensation under the Employees' Compensation Act, 1923 and is in breach of the OSH Code, 2020.
whatToDoIfViolated:
1. File a complaint with the Labour Commissioner / Inspector-cum-Facilitator under the OSH Code.
2. For sexual harassment, file a complaint with the Internal Complaints Committee (ICC) within 3 months.
3. If no ICC exists, approach the Local Complaints Committee (LCC) at the District Officer's office.
4. For workplace injury, claim compensation under the Employees' Compensation Act, 1923.
5. Contact the National Commission for Women at 7827-170-170 for POSH Act violations.
6. Approach the Labour Court for recovery of compensation.
7. Seek free legal aid through DLSA (call NALSA 15100).

title: Right to Equal Pay for Equal Work
summary: No employer can pay different wages to men and women for the same work. The principle of equal pay for equal work is a constitutional right under Article 39(d).
body:
The principle of **equal pay for equal work** is a Directive Principle under **Article 39(d)** of the Constitution and has been held by the Supreme Court to be a fundamental right enforceable under Article 14 and Article 16. The principle is implemented through the **Code on Wages, 2019** (which subsumes the Equal Remuneration Act, 1976) and the Minimum Wages Act, 1948 (until the Code is fully notified).

**What the law says:**
1. The **Equal Remuneration Act, 1976** (Sections 4 and 5) prohibits paying a woman less than a man for the same work or work of similar nature, and prohibits discrimination in recruitment for the same work.
2. The **Code on Wages, 2019** consolidates these provisions (Chapter on Equal Remuneration) — to be fully notified.
3. The principle extends to bonus, overtime, and other remuneration — these must be paid equally to men and women for the same work.
4. Maternity benefits cannot be counted as 'extra pay' to women employees — they are statutory rights under the Maternity Benefit Act, 1961.

**Who is covered?** All employees in the organised and unorganised sector — the Code covers both public and private establishments irrespective of employee strength.

**Landmark judgments:**
- *MacKinnon Mackenzie & Co. Ltd. v. Audrey D'Costa* (1987) 2 SCC 469: Female stenographers must be paid the same wage as male stenotypists when the work is similar.
- *State of Punjab v. Jagjit Singh* (1996) 11 SCC 1: Temporary employees doing the same work as permanent employees are entitled to equal pay, subject to identical recruitment rules.
- *State of Haryana v. Tilak Raj* (2003) 4 SCC 335: Different pay scales for similar work can be justified only on grounds of recruitment source or different qualifications.

**Conditions for claiming equal pay:**
1. The work must be the **same or of similar nature** — requiring similar skill, effort, and responsibility.
2. Performed under **similar working conditions**.
3. The disparity in pay cannot be justified on grounds of **different qualifications, experience, or seniority**.

**Casual and contract workers:** The principle of equal pay for equal work applies to daily-wage, casual, and contract workers as well — the Supreme Court in *State of Punjab v. Surinder Kumar* (1986) 4 SCC 636 extended it to daily-wage workers. However, courts have allowed some differentiation between regularised and temporary workers if there is a rational basis (e.g., different recruitment method).

**Gender pay gap and the law:**
1. The Equal Remuneration Act / Code on Wages prohibits paying a woman less than a man for the same work.
2. Employers cannot lower a woman's wages after she returns from maternity leave.
3. Piece-rate wages must be calculated equally for men and women.

If a worker is paid less than colleagues of the opposite gender for the same work: 1. Demand equal wages in writing. 2. File a complaint with the Labour Commissioner under the Equal Remuneration Act, 1976 / Code on Wages, 2019. 3. Approach the Inspector under the Minimum Wages Act. 4. File a case in the Labour Court. 5. Approach the National Commission for Women (NCW) at 7827-170-170. 6. Seek free legal aid through DLSA.
actualLaw: Article 39(d) of the Constitution of India; Code on Wages, 2019; Equal Remuneration Act, 1976 (Sections 4 and 5)
example: A woman and a man are both employed as data entry operators doing the same work, but the woman is paid less. This violates the Equal Remuneration Act, 1976 and Article 39(d) of the Constitution.
whatToDoIfViolated:
1. Demand equal wages in writing from the employer.
2. File a complaint with the Labour Commissioner under the Equal Remuneration Act, 1976 / Code on Wages, 2019.
3. Approach the Inspector under the Minimum Wages Act, 1948.
4. File a case in the Labour Court for recovery of unpaid wages and damages.
5. Approach the National Commission for Women at 7827-170-170.
6. Seek free legal aid through DLSA (call NALSA 15100).

title: Right to Safe and Quality Goods
summary: Consumers have the right to goods that are safe, of merchantable quality, and free from defects. Hazardous goods must carry warnings and can be recalled at the manufacturer's cost.
body:
The **Consumer Protection Act, 2019 (CPA 2019)** gives every consumer the right to be protected against marketing of goods and services that are hazardous to life and property. This is one of the **six consumer rights** recognised under Section 2(9) of the Act.

**The six consumer rights (Section 2(9), CPA 2019):**
1. Right to be protected against marketing of goods/services hazardous to life and property.
2. Right to be informed about the quality, quantity, potency, purity, standard, and price of goods.
3. Right to be assured of access to a variety of goods at competitive prices.
4. Right to be heard and to be assured that consumer interests will receive due consideration.
5. Right to seek redressal against unfair trade practices or restrictive trade practices.
6. Right to consumer education.

**Duties of the manufacturer / seller:**
1. Goods must conform to the **BIS standards / ISI mark / FSSAI standards** where applicable.
2. Provide clear instructions and warnings for safe use of the product.
3. Maintain quality control — defective batches must be recalled at the manufacturer's cost.
4. Not engage in **unfair trade practices** — false claims, misleading advertisements, fake reviews.
5. Provide warranty / guarantee on goods as advertised.
6. Refund or replace goods that do not conform to the express terms of warranty.

**Product liability (Sections 84–87, CPA 2019):**
- A manufacturer, product seller, or service provider is liable for harm caused by a **defective product**.
- The complainant can claim: (a) refund of price, (b) compensation for any injury or loss, (c) return of the defective product, (d) medical expenses if the product caused injury.
- The product manufacturer can be held liable for: (i) manufacturing defect, (ii) design defect, (iii) deviation from manufacturing specifications, (iv) failure to give adequate warnings, (v) non-conformity with express warranty.

**Recall of hazardous goods:**
- The **Central Consumer Protection Authority (CCPA)**, constituted under Section 10 of the CPA 2019, can order recall of hazardous goods, refund of price, and discontinuance of unfair trade practices (Section 20).
- The CCPA can also impose penalties for misleading advertisements — up to ₹10 lakh for the first offence, and up to ₹50 lakh for subsequent offences (Section 21).

**Food safety:**
- The **Food Safety and Standards Act, 2006** (administered by FSSAI) regulates food products — labelling, packaging, additives, expiry, and recall.
- Complaints about adulterated or unsafe food can be filed at **foodlicensing.fssai.gov.in** or with the State Food Safety Commissioner.

**Drugs and cosmetics:**
- The **Drugs and Cosmetics Act, 1940** regulates manufacture, sale, and distribution of drugs and cosmetics.
- Spurious / adulterated drugs are a criminal offence punishable with imprisonment up to life.

**What constitutes a defect?**
1. The product does not perform as advertised.
2. The product is unsafe when used as intended.
3. The product has manufacturing flaws.
4. The product does not meet the warranty terms.
5. The product is past its expiry date.
6. The product is wrongly labelled (e.g., wrong MRP, wrong country of origin).

If you have bought unsafe or defective goods: 1. Preserve the bill, packaging, and the product itself. 2. File a complaint with the seller / grievance officer. 3. File a complaint with the District Consumer Commission under Section 35 of the CPA, 2019 — claims up to ₹50 lakh. 4. For hazard to public safety, file a complaint with the CCPA. 5. File through e-Daakhil (edaakhil.nic.in). 6. Call the National Consumer Helpline 1915.
actualLaw: Consumer Protection Act, 2019 (Sections 2(9), 10, 20, 21, 35, 84–87); Food Safety and Standards Act, 2006; Drugs and Cosmetics Act, 1940
example: A consumer buys an electric kettle that explodes due to a manufacturing defect, causing burns. The manufacturer is liable for product liability under Section 84 of the CPA, 2019.
whatToDoIfViolated:
1. Preserve the bill, packaging, and the product itself.
2. File a complaint with the seller / grievance officer in writing.
3. File a complaint with the District Consumer Commission under Section 35 of the CPA, 2019.
4. For hazard to public safety, complain to the CCPA at consumerhelpline.gov.in.
5. File online at edaakhil.nic.in.
6. Call National Consumer Helpline 1915.
7. For food / drugs, complain to FSSAI or State Drug Controller.

title: E-commerce Returns and Refunds Rights
summary: Online shoppers have the right to return products within the stipulated window and receive refunds to the original payment method within a reasonable time.
body:
The **Consumer Protection (E-Commerce) Rules, 2020**, notified under the Consumer Protection Act, 2019, regulate the conduct of e-commerce entities like Amazon, Flipkart, Myntra, Swiggy, Zomato, and others. They give consumers specific rights regarding returns, refunds, and grievance redressal.

**Your rights to return goods (Rule 4 of the E-Commerce Rules, 2020):**
1. E-commerce entities must not refuse to take back goods or withdraw services, or fail to refund consideration paid, where the goods or services are defective, deficient, or different from what was advertised.
2. Returns and refunds must be made within the stipulated time — typically the platform's stated return window (7 to 14 days for most categories).
3. Refunds must be paid to the **original payment method** — i.e., the credit/debit card, UPI account, or bank account used for the transaction.
4. The platform cannot force the consumer to accept store credit or wallet balance instead of a refund to the original payment method.
5. For COD (Cash on Delivery) orders, the consumer must be refunded via UPI / bank transfer / cheque — not just wallet credit.

**Mandatory disclosures by e-commerce entities (Rule 4(3)):**
1. Legal name, principal geographic address, contact details (email, phone).
2. **Grievance Officer** details — name, designation, email, contact number. Complaints must be acknowledged within **48 hours** and resolved within **1 month** (Rule 4(4)).
3. Country of origin of all products at the pre-purchase stage.
4. Complete product information — ingredients, batch, MRP, manufacture/expiry date, customer care details, return policy, warranty, exchange policy.
5. Total price (including all taxes), delivery charges, and any other fees at the pre-purchase stage.

**What is banned (Rule 5)?**
1. Importing goods that violate IP laws.
2. Selling goods that are unsafe, substandard, or incorrectly labelled.
3. Manipulating prices unfairly during festive sales or 'flash sales'.
4. Using fake reviews or misleading social media endorsements.
5. Charging for free samples or trial products.

**Sellers' and platforms' liability:**
1. The seller (vendor on the marketplace) is liable for defective products.
2. The marketplace platform is liable if it exercises control over inventory, pricing, or delivery (inventory-based model).
3. For misleading advertisements, both the seller, the endorser, and (in some cases) the platform can be held liable.

**Chargeback rights:** If paid by credit/debit card, the consumer can file a **chargeback** with their bank under the RBI's card-issuance regulations — typically within 90–120 days of the transaction. The bank reverses the payment if the dispute is established.

**Food delivery (Swiggy, Zomato, etc.):**
1. If the food is delivered cold, wrong, spilled, or different from the menu description, the consumer is entitled to refund / replacement.
2. The platform's grievance officer must respond within 48 hours.
3. For adulterated or unsafe food, complain to FSSAI at foodlicensing.fssai.gov.in.

**Quick Commerce (Blinkit, Zepto, Instamart):**
1. Items with short expiry must be flagged at the time of order.
2. Wrong or missing items must be refunded within the stated timeline.
3. Refunds cannot be forced into platform wallet — the consumer must be offered the original payment method.

If your return or refund request is denied: 1. File a complaint with the Grievance Officer of the platform (must respond within 48 hours, resolve within 1 month). 2. Call the National Consumer Helpline 1915. 3. File a complaint online at edaakhil.nic.in (District Commission up to ₹50 lakh; State Commission ₹50 lakh to ₹2 crore; NCDRC above ₹2 crore). 4. For financial fraud, call 1930 within 24 hours. 5. File a chargeback with your bank if paid by card.
actualLaw: Consumer Protection (E-Commerce) Rules, 2020 (Rules 4 and 5); Consumer Protection Act, 2019; RBI Cardholder Regulations (for chargebacks)
example: An online shopper returns a defective phone within 7 days. The seller offers only wallet credit, not refund to the original card. This violates Rule 4 of the E-Commerce Rules, 2020.
whatToDoIfViolated:
1. File a complaint with the e-commerce platform's Grievance Officer (acknowledged within 48 hours, resolved within 1 month).
2. Call the National Consumer Helpline 1915.
3. File a complaint at edaakhil.nic.in (District / State / National Commission based on claim value).
4. File a chargeback with your bank if paid by card (within 90–120 days).
5. For financial fraud, call 1930 and report at cybercrime.gov.in.
6. For adulterated food, complain to FSSAI at foodlicensing.fssai.gov.in.

title: Right to Be Forgotten (Erasure of Personal Data)
summary: Under the DPDP Act 2023, you can ask a company to erase your personal data once the purpose for which it was collected is served. Court-ordered de-indexing of personal information from search results is also recognised.
body:
The **right to be forgotten** — the right to have one's personal data erased — is recognised in India under the **Digital Personal Data Protection (DPDP) Act, 2023** and through judicial pronouncements by the High Courts and the Supreme Court under Article 21 (right to privacy).

**What the DPDP Act, 2023 says (Section 12):**
1. A **Data Principal** (the individual to whom the personal data relates) has the right to erasure of personal data and withdrawal of consent.
2. The Data Principal can ask the **Data Fiduciary** (any company or platform holding the data) to erase the personal data — this right is sometimes called the 'right to be forgotten'.
3. The Data Fiduciary must comply unless retention is required by law (e.g., to comply with a court order, KYC norms under the PMLA, or for a pending legal claim).
4. The Data Fiduciary must also erase data from any **Data Processor** (e.g., cloud provider) it has shared the data with.
5. The right is balanced against **legitimate purposes** — including the right to freedom of speech and expression of others.

**Limits of the right:**
1. The Data Fiduciary can refuse erasure if the data is necessary for:
   - Compliance with a judgment or order of any court or tribunal.
   - Compliance with any law in force in India (e.g., KYC records under the PMLA, tax records under the IT Act).
   - To respond to a lawful claim.
   - For research, archiving, or statistical purposes in the public interest.
2. The right is **not absolute** — the Data Protection Board (to be constituted under the DPDP Act) can adjudicate disputes.

**Judicial recognition:**
- The **Karnataka High Court** in *Sri Vasunathan v. The Registrar General, High Court of Karnataka* (2017) recognised the right to be forgotten under Article 21 — protecting a woman's name from appearing in a published judgment affecting her reputation.
- The **Madras High Court** in *K. Karthikeyan v. The Registrar General, Madras High Court* (2021) declined an absolute right to be forgotten but allowed for **masking** of personal information in published judgments.
- The Supreme Court in *Justice K.S. Puttaswamy v. Union of India* (2017) 10 SCC 1 recognised the **right to privacy** as a fundamental right — a basis for the right to be forgotten.

**Search engine de-indexing:**
- An individual can request search engines (Google, Bing) to remove specific URLs containing personal information — Google has an online form for this.
- For non-consensual intimate images (revenge porn), Google will de-index quickly under its policies.
- For outdated or inaccurate information, the platform may be ordered by a court to remove the content.

**Right against reputation damage:**
- Even where the right to be forgotten is not available, the individual has remedies under the **defamation provisions of the BNS, 2023 (Sections 351, 352)** and tort law.
- For removal of false / defamatory online content, the IT Act's **intermediary guidelines (IT Rules, 2021)** require intermediaries to remove content within 36 hours of a court order or government direction.

If your data has been unlawfully retained or published: 1. Send a written request to the Data Fiduciary (the company / platform) seeking erasure under Section 12 of the DPDP Act, 2023. 2. If refused, file a complaint with the **Data Protection Board** (to be constituted under the DPDP Act). 3. For defamatory online content, send a court order or notice to the intermediary (search engine / platform). 4. For intimate images posted without consent, complain at cybercrime.gov.in or call 1930. 5. Approach the High Court under Article 226 for de-indexing of personal information from search results.
actualLaw: Section 12, Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023; Article 21, Constitution of India; Information Technology (Intermediary Guidelines and Digital Media Ethics Code) Rules, 2021; Sections 351 and 352, Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (defamation)
example: A person's name appears in an old court judgment published online, affecting their job prospects. They can approach the High Court for masking of their name in the published judgment.
whatToDoIfViolated:
1. Send a written request to the Data Fiduciary seeking erasure under Section 12 of the DPDP Act, 2023.
2. If refused, file a complaint with the Data Protection Board.
3. For defamatory content, send a court order or notice to the intermediary (search engine / platform).
4. For intimate images posted without consent, complain at cybercrime.gov.in or call 1930.
5. Approach the High Court under Article 226 for de-indexing of personal information.
6. Seek free legal aid through DLSA.

title: Social Media User Rights in India
summary: Social media users have the right to free speech on platforms, the right to be informed before account suspension, and the right to grievance redressal within 15 days. Platforms must comply with Indian law.
body:
The **Information Technology Act, 2000** and the **Information Technology (Intermediary Guidelines and Digital Media Ethics Code) Rules, 2021** (commonly called the **IT Rules 2021**) regulate social media intermediaries like WhatsApp, Facebook, Instagram, X (Twitter), YouTube, and Telegram in India.

**What is an intermediary?** Section 2(1)(w) of the IT Act defines an intermediary as any person who receives, stores, or transmits electronic records on behalf of others — including social media platforms, messaging apps, search engines, and cloud services.

**Safe harbour protection (Section 79, IT Act):**
1. Intermediaries are not liable for third-party content posted on their platforms, provided they comply with due-diligence requirements.
2. They must not initiate the transmission, select the receiver, or modify the content.
3. They must observe due diligence and follow guidelines issued by the government.
4. They must remove unlawful content within **36 hours** of a court order or government direction.

**Duties of Significant Social Media Intermediaries (SSMIs) — those with 50 lakh+ users (Rule 4):**
1. Appoint a **Chief Compliance Officer** (resident of India) to ensure compliance with the IT Act and Rules.
2. Appoint a **Nodal Contact Person** (resident of India) for 24x7 coordination with law-enforcement agencies.
3. Appoint a **Resident Grievance Officer** (resident of India) to handle complaints — name and contact must be displayed on the platform.
4. Publish a **monthly compliance report** with details of complaints received and action taken.
5. Enable **identification of the originator** of messages on messaging platforms (e.g., WhatsApp) — but only on a court order or order of a competent authority under Section 69A of the IT Act.
6. Remove unlawful content within 36 hours of receiving an order.

**Your rights as a user (Rule 3):**
1. **Right to be informed**: The platform must publish its terms of service, privacy policy, and user agreement.
2. **Right to grievance redressal**: The Grievance Officer must acknowledge a complaint within **24 hours** and resolve it within **15 days** (Rule 3(2)).
3. **Right to be heard before suspension**: A user must be given a notice and a reasonable opportunity to be heard before their account is disabled or suspended, except in cases where the platform acts on a court / government order or for urgent removal of unlawful content (Rule 3(1)(d)).
4. **Right to reasons**: The platform must give reasons for removing content or suspending an account.
5. **Right to appeal**: If dissatisfied, the user can appeal to the **Grievance Appellate Committee (GAC)** constituted by the government under Rule 3A.

**Prohibited content (Rule 3(1)(b)):**
1. Content that is defamatory, obscene, pornographic, paedophilic, invasive of another's privacy.
2. Content that harms minors in any way.
3. Content that infringes IP rights.
4. Content that is misleading, fraudulent, or impersonates another person.
5. Content that threatens the unity, integrity, defence, security, or sovereignty of India.
6. Content that violates any law in force.

**Content removal and Section 69A of the IT Act:**
1. The Government can issue blocking orders for content that affects sovereignty, security, friendly relations with foreign states, or public order.
2. Blocking orders must follow the procedure under the **Blocking Rules, 2009** (Information Technology (Procedure and Safeguards for Blocking for Access of Information by Public) Rules, 2009).
3. The Supreme Court in *Shreya Singhal v. Union of India* (2015) 5 SCC 1 struck down Section 66A of the IT Act as unconstitutional and clarified that blocking orders must be by written order with reasons.

**Voluntary self-regulation:**
1. Content standards for OTT (streaming) platforms are set under the IT Rules 2021 and self-regulatory bodies (e.g., the Digital Publishers Content Grievances Council).
2. For digital news media, additional compliance with the Press Council of India's norms applies.

If your content is removed or your account is suspended unfairly: 1. Contact the platform's Grievance Officer — the platform must respond within 15 days. 2. Appeal to the **Grievance Appellate Committee (GAC)** at the Ministry of Electronics and IT within 30 days of the platform's decision. 3. For violation of free speech, file a writ petition in the High Court under Article 226. 4. For defamatory content, contact the platform for removal (Section 79 IT Act). 5. For criminal content, file a complaint at cybercrime.gov.in.
actualLaw: Sections 79 and 69A, Information Technology Act, 2000; Information Technology (Intermediary Guidelines and Digital Media Ethics Code) Rules, 2021; Shreya Singhal v. Union of India (2015) 5 SCC 1
example: A user's X (Twitter) account is suspended without a prior notice. They can file a complaint with the platform's Grievance Officer and, if unresolved, appeal to the Grievance Appellate Committee (GAC) within 30 days.
whatToDoIfViolated:
1. Contact the platform's Grievance Officer — the platform must respond within 15 days.
2. Appeal to the Grievance Appellate Committee (GAC) within 30 days of the platform's decision.
3. For violation of free speech, file a writ petition in the High Court under Article 226.
4. For defamatory content, contact the platform for removal.
5. For criminal content, file a complaint at cybercrime.gov.in.
6. Seek free legal aid through DLSA.

title: Right Against Abandonment and Abuse
summary: Abandoning or abusing a senior citizen is a criminal offence under the BNS, 2023. The MWPSC Act, 2007 protects senior citizens against physical, emotional, and financial abuse.
body:
Abandonment, neglect, and abuse of senior citizens is both a criminal offence and a violation of their statutory rights. The **Maintenance and Welfare of Parents and Senior Citizens Act, 2007** (amended in 2023) and the **Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS)** provide criminal and civil remedies.

**Criminal law — BNS, 2023:**
1. **Section 115 BNS** — voluntarily causing hurt (corresponds to old IPC Section 323). Applies to physical abuse of a senior.
2. **Section 125 BNS** — wrongful confinement (corresponds to old IPC Section 340). Applies where a senior is locked in a room.
3. **Section 316 BNS** — criminal breach of trust (corresponds to old IPC Section 405). Applies where a son or caregiver misuses the parent's pension or funds.
4. **Section 318 BNS** — cheating (corresponds to old IPC Section 415). Applies to grabbing a senior's property by deception.
5. **Section 351 BNS** — defamation (corresponds to old IPC Section 499). Applies to verbal abuse harming reputation.

**MWPSC Act, 2007 — Protection against abuse:**
1. The Maintenance Tribunal (SDM office) has powers to pass orders for the protection of life and property of senior citizens.
2. **Section 23** — if a senior citizen has transferred property to a child or relative on the condition that they will be taken care of, and the child/relative subsequently neglects or fails to provide care, the senior citizen can declare the transfer void. This is a powerful remedy — it reverses the property transfer.
3. The Tribunal can issue protection orders restraining children / relatives from harassing, evicting, or disposing of the senior citizen's property.
4. The Maintenance Tribunal (SDM office) is the first point of contact for both maintenance and protection matters.

**What constitutes abandonment / abuse?**
1. **Physical abuse**: hitting, slapping, pushing, restraining, denying food or medication.
2. **Emotional abuse**: verbal abuse, isolation, threats, humiliation.
3. **Financial abuse**: misappropriating pension, forcing property transfer, forging wills, denying access to bank accounts.
4. **Neglect**: failure to provide food, clothing, shelter, medical care, or basic amenities.
5. **Abandonment**: leaving a senior citizen in a public place, hospital, or old-age home without consent.
6. **Eviction**: forcing a senior out of their own house.

**Who is liable?**
1. Adult children (son, daughter).
2. Grandchildren (in the absence of children).
3. Legal heirs of a deceased child.
4. Caregivers (paid or unpaid) — under criminal law.
5. Guardians or attorneys under a Power of Attorney who misuse the position.

**Helplines and authorities:**
1. **Elders Helpline — 14567** (national toll-free, 24x7).
2. **Maintenance Tribunal (SDM office)** — for maintenance and protection orders.
3. **NALSA — 15100** for free legal aid.
4. **NHRC — 14433** for human rights violations.
5. **Women's Helpline — 181** for senior women facing abuse.
6. **Police — 100** for immediate physical danger.
7. **Senior Citizen Police Helpline** — most states have a dedicated number.

**Specialised protections:**
1. **Reverse Mortgage Act, 2007** — seniors can mortgage their house to a bank for monthly payments, while continuing to live there.
2. **Old Age Pension** — IGNOAPS (₹200–₹500/month for BPL seniors 60+); state top-ups.
3. **Indira Gandhi National Widow Pension Scheme (IGNWPS)** — ₹300/month for BPL widows 40–79.
4. **Indira Gandhi National Disability Pension Scheme (IGNDPS)** — ₹300/month for BPL persons with severe disabilities 18–79.
5. **Annapurna Scheme** — free food grains for BPL seniors not covered under IGNOAPS.

If a senior citizen is being abused or abandoned: 1. Call 14567 (Elders Helpline) or 100 (Police) for immediate danger. 2. Approach the Maintenance Tribunal (SDM office) for protection orders. 3. File an FIR under the relevant sections of BNS, 2023. 4. Seek free legal aid from NALSA at 15100. 5. Approach the NHRC at 14433 for human rights violations. 6. Apply for state old-age pension if not already receiving.

example: A son forces his elderly mother to transfer her property to him and then evicts her. He can be prosecuted under BNS Section 318 (cheating) and the property transfer can be declared void under Section 23 of the MWPSC Act, 2007.
whatToDoIfViolated:
1. Call 14567 (Elders Helpline) or 100 (Police) for immediate danger.
2. Approach the Maintenance Tribunal (SDM office) for protection orders.
3. File an FIR under BNS Sections 115, 125, 316, 318, 351 (as applicable).
4. Approach NALSA helpline 15100 for free legal aid.
5. Approach NHRC at 14433 for human rights violations.
6. Apply for Old Age Pension Scheme in your state.
7. If property transferred, file for declaration of transfer as void under Section 23 of the MWPSC Act, 2007.

title: Right to Healthcare and Old Age Pension
summary: Senior citizens have the right to free or subsidised healthcare, priority access in hospitals, and old-age pension under central and state schemes.
body:
Senior citizens (60+ years) have statutory rights to healthcare, priority access in hospitals, and social security pensions under the **Maintenance and Welfare of Parents and Senior Citizens Act, 2007** (MWPSC Act), the **National Policy on Older Persons, 1999**, and the **Maintenance and Welfare of Parents and Senior Citizens (Amendment) Act, 2023**.

**Right to healthcare under the MWPSC Act, 2007 (Section 20):**
1. State Governments must ensure that Government hospitals partially or fully reimburse medical expenses of senior citizens (eligible for maintenance) when their children or relatives fail to meet the medical expenses.
2. Hospitals must provide separate queues for senior citizens for consultation and admission.
3. Facility for treatment of geriatric patients in every district hospital, with beds reserved for them.
4. Home care facilities for seniors who cannot travel to hospital.
5. The 2023 amendment expands these provisions to include domiciliary care and palliative care.

**Right to old age pension — central schemes:**
1. **Indira Gandhi National Old Age Pension Scheme (IGNOAPS)** under the National Social Assistance Programme (NSAP):
   - Eligibility: BPL persons aged 60+.
   - Amount: ₹200/month for 60–79 years; ₹500/month for 80+ years.
   - Many states provide a top-up (e.g., ₹1,000–₹2,500/month depending on the state).
2. **Indira Gandhi National Widow Pension Scheme (IGNWPS)**:
   - BPL widows aged 40–79 years.
   - ₹300/month; state top-ups apply.
3. **Indira Gandhi National Disability Pension Scheme (IGNDPS)**:
   - BPL persons with severe (80%+) disability aged 18–79.
   - ₹300/month.
4. **Annapurna Scheme** — 10 kg of free food grains per month for BPL seniors not covered under the pension scheme (subsumed under PMGKAY in many states).
5. **Ayushman Bharat PM-JAY** — ₹5 lakh/year health cover for BPL families. Some states have extended it to all senior citizens (60+) in their state.

**State schemes:**
- Most states have their own old age pension (e.g., Delhi, Kerala, Tamil Nadu, Andhra Pradesh) — amounts vary from ₹1,000 to ₹2,500/month.
- Many states have free bus travel for seniors.
- Some states (Tamil Nadu, Andhra Pradesh) have free or subsidised medical insurance for seniors.

**Right to reverse mortgage:**
- The **Reverse Mortgage Act, 2007** allows seniors to mortgage their house to a bank in exchange for monthly payments while continuing to live in the property.
- No repayment is due until the senior dies or permanently moves out.
- Available from major banks — SBI, PNB, Bank of Baroda.

**Right to priority in public services:**
1. **Air travel** — seniors 60+ are entitled to wheelchair assistance on demand and priority check-in.
2. **Railways** — separate counters, lower berths in trains, concession in fares (some concessions have been withdrawn post-COVID).
3. **Hospitals** — separate queue, priority consultation.
4. **Banks** — separate counters for seniors (RBI mandate).
5. **Telecom** — BSNL offers special plans for seniors.
6. **Courts** — priority listing of cases involving seniors.

**Right against denial of emergency medical treatment:**
1. The **Supreme Court in Paschim Banga Khet Mazdoor Samity v. State of West Bengal (1996) 4 SCC 37** held that denial of emergency medical treatment violates Article 21 of the Constitution.
2. The **Clinical Establishments (Registration and Regulation) Act, 2010** (applicable in some states) requires hospitals to provide emergency stabilisation before transfer.
3. **Charter of Patient Rights** (Ministry of Health, 2018) — guarantees right to information, second opinion, and refusal of unnecessary treatment.

If denied healthcare or pension: 1. Approach the District Social Welfare Officer / District Magistrate for old age pension. 2. Approach the District Health Society / Chief Medical Officer for hospital-related issues. 3. File an RTI application to know the status of the pension. 4. Approach the State Human Rights Commission for denial of healthcare. 5. Approach the Maintenance Tribunal (SDM) for medical reimbursement under Section 20 of the MWPSC Act. 6. Call 14567 (Elders Helpline) for guidance. 7. Seek free legal aid from NALSA at 15100.

State of West Bengal (1996) 4 SCC 37

2. Approach the District Health Society / Chief Medical Officer for hospital-related issues.
3. File an RTI application to know the status of the pension.
4. Approach the State Human Rights Commission for denial of healthcare.
